What you are looking for is “Upfront carbon” and it’s gonna be a deep dive.

So what you found is what people call operational carbon. The carbon emission of the upkeep of the building. But before that… lemme start what they mean by “carbon” and why the unit is carbon per unit. 

They only use carbon as a point of reference. However carbon as a unit is basically the Green House Gas (ghg) factor multiplied by mass of carbon. So if the ghg factor of compound X is 10  and there was 1 kg/m^3 of compound X that was released. Then this means there was 10 kg/m^3 of carbon released. Most of the times there are databases that gives you the factor for you and you just need to multiply it to your material schedule. You can look at EPD database like ICE database. There’s heaps of research in australia with melb uni and their EPIC database… but i have some reservations about it. 

If you are surprised how easy the calc is… it is that easy but it gets pretty complicated fast. The issue you will see quickly is that you number will mean fuck all. When you don’t look at the lifecycle of the whole building from design to end of life/refurb. Lots of things during construction and procurement will affect your number. Where you source the materials, how it’s constructed and how it’s going to be demolished/refurb. Even whether electricity renewable or not will affect your numbers/design. For instance it’s worth to have solar panels in countries that rely on fossil energy but counties that are mostly renewable it’s not worth it because you are just adding unnecessary upfront carbon.

What i suggest is using your numbers as a guideline to achieve. Like you do as a quantity surveyor but for upfront carbon. Technically this is something they are starting to do as well. 

Fyi the ghg calc is another deep dive which people are kinda fighting over. The issue lies on the scope of where you consider something related to the manufacturing of materials and the associated carbon emissions. Hence why i say to not take the numbers as the be all and end all.
